reason: The sources provide over 15 highly detailed, cross-verified claims about the Voyager Golden Record's radioactive uranium clock, its physical construction, and its journey.
story: In 1977, NASA launched the twin Voyager spacecraft carrying a golden message to the stars. Bolted to each probe is the Voyager Golden Record, a gold-plated copper disk filled with Earth's sounds, music, and images. But how would an alien finder know how long this cosmic bottle has been drifting? To solve this, scientists placed a mind-bending clock on the record's aluminum cover: an ultra-pure sample of radioactive uranium-238. Because uranium-238 decays steadily with a half-life of about 4.5 billion years, any advanced civilization that intercepts the probe can measure the remaining uranium and its decay products. This allows them to calculate exactly when the spacecraft left Earth. Alongside a cosmic map of pulsars, this silent radioactive clock serves as a physical timestamp, ensuring that even if humanity is long gone, the universe will know exactly when we reached out.
angle: The Voyager Golden Record's cover carries an ultra-pure sample of radioactive uranium-238, which acts as a silent atomic clock allowing aliens to calculate exactly when the spacecraft was launched.

claims.claim: The Voyager Golden Records are two identical phonograph records launched aboard twin Voyager spacecraft in 1977.
Both Voyager probes have entered interstellar space.
The creation and content selection of the Golden Record was led by astronomer Carl Sagan.
Ann Druyan was a key member of the team that created the record's content.
The Golden Record contains spoken greetings in 55 languages.
The record includes natural sounds of Earth, including humpback whale songs.
The Golden Record is a 12-inch copper disk plated with nickel and gold.
The record's protective cover is made of aluminum.
An ultra-pure sample of the isotope uranium-238 is electroplated onto the cover of the record.
The uranium-238 sample electroplated onto the cover has a low radioactivity of about 0.00026 microcuries.
Uranium-238 decays with a half-life of approximately 4.5 billion years.
Finders can measure the ratio of remaining uranium-238 to daughter isotopes as a radioactive clock to calculate its age.
The record cover features a drawing of the record and stylus showing how to play it.
The cover uses binary notation to state the correct rotation speed of 3.6 seconds.
The cover features a pulsar map showing the Solar System's location relative to 14 pulsars to help date the launch era.
The cover includes a drawing of the hydrogen atom in its two lowest states to establish a fundamental time scale.
The hand-etched message 'To the makers of music – all worlds, all times' was written in the record's run-out groove.
NASA initially rejected the records due to the unauthorized inscription until Sagan successfully intervened.
The Morse code message 'Ad astra per aspera' is included on the record.
Voyager 1 will pass near another star in about 40,000 years.

disputed: Whether the Beatles song 'Here Comes the Sun' was blocked by EMI copyright (supported by S1 and S6) or was never seriously considered for inclusion as recalled by Timothy Ferris (supported by S1). The script should present both sides or leave it out.

The identity of the star Voyager 1 will approach in 40,000 years: S1 identifies it as Gliese 445 at 1.6 light-years, while S6 identifies it as AC+79 3888 at 1.7 light-years. The script should refer generally to 'a nearby star' and omit specific names and distances.
The exact half-life of Uranium-238: S1 states 4.468 billion years, S2 states 4.51 billion years, and S7 mentions both. The script should state 'about 4.5 billion years'.
